analysis.one_liner: Bans Canadian wheat imports until Canada reopens its market to US durum wheat.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past the Senate Finance Committee and died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: Canada banned US durum wheat imports after a karnal bunt fungus outbreak in Arizona, including wheat from northern states where the fungus was never found. This bill would direct the President to ban all Canadian wheat and grain imports until Canada lifted its ban and certified that US durum wheat had fair access to Canadian markets. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received any further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Wheat farmers in the northern Plains, especially durum wheat growers in North Dakota and Montana, who were shut out of the Canadian market by Canada's ban. If the retaliation worked, they would regain export sales; whether or not it worked, blocking Canadian wheat would reduce competition and support domestic grain prices.

how_it_helps.text: The bill directs the President to prohibit entry of all Canadian wheat and wheat-flour products within 15 days of enactment, with the ban to stay in place until the Secretary of Agriculture and the US Trade Representative determine and certify to Congress that Canada has lifted its ban on US durum wheat from areas without evidence of karnal bunt.

The bill's findings state that Canada's ban covered all US durum wheat, including wheat from states where no karnal bunt had been found, and that Canada itself said its cold climate posed no outbreak risk — the basis for calling the ban unjustifiable.

By cutting off Canadian competition in the US grain market, the ban would put upward pressure on prices received by US wheat growers, including producers in North Dakota, Montana, South Dakota, Minnesota, and the Great Lakes region named in the findings.

analysis.who_pays: American consumers, who would pay more for grain-based foods; US flour millers and bakers, who would lose Canadian wheat supplies and face higher input costs; Canadian grain exporters, who would lose access to the US market; and potentially other US exporters if Canada retaliated.

drawbacks.text: The ban covers all Canadian wheat and flour regardless of origin, mirroring the same overbreadth the bill criticized in Canada's ban — it would block grain from all of Canada even though the bill's own findings say karnal bunt had never been found in northern US states, let alone proven in Canadian grain.

Blocking imports of a staple commodity tends to raise domestic prices: US millers would lose Canadian wheat supplies and those costs would be passed to consumers buying bread, pasta, and other grain products.
A blanket retaliation against Canadian grain could invite Canadian counter-retaliation against other US exports, widening a dispute over one crop into a broader trade fight.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The leverage argument is real: Canada's ban did block US durum wheat from regions with no evidence of the fungus, and a retaliatory ban is the classic tool for forcing a trading partner back to the table. But the costs are spread broadly — every grain consumer and miller pays more — while the benefit is concentrated on one group of growers, and if Canada did not back down the ban would just be a self-imposed price increase with no payoff.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, and the bill died there when the 104th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Kent Conrad of North Dakota introduced the bill on March 28, 1996, in response to Canada's ban on US durum wheat imports imposed after a karnal bunt outbreak in Arizona.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance, the committee with jurisdiction over tariff and trade measures.
No further action was ever recorded — no committee markup, no hearing, no floor vote — and the bill expired at the end of the 104th Congress on January 3, 1997.
It had a single cosponsor and never attracted broader recorded support in the Senate.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Canadian grain exporters kept full access to the US market, and American consumers and flour millers were spared the higher grain prices a ban would have caused. Northern Plains durum growers, the intended beneficiaries, stayed locked out of the Canadian market.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Canadian exporters, US consumers and millers

for.name: Sen. Kent Conrad
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

against.name: Sen. William V. Roth Jr.
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred to the Finance Committee; no markup or hearing was ever held and the bill died there.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes on the bill and only two senators are recorded in support — both Democrats from the wheat-growing region — so no partisan split on the merits is visible in the record.

industries.note: The bill would cut off Canadian wheat competition to pressure Canada into reopening its market, and would prop up domestic prices in the meantime. The benefit is concentrated on growers while the cost — higher grain and flour prices — spreads to everyone who eats.
A total ban on Canadian wheat and flour would close off their largest export market until their government conceded. Their loss is the point of the bill.

Millers and food manufacturers rely on grain supplies, and losing Canadian wheat would raise their input costs — costs that get passed to consumers, so their interest here runs alongside the public's.
